summary: Presents a YANG 1.1 module defining identities, typedefs, and groupings useful to cryptographic applications.

eli5.summary: This provides ready-made building blocks for describing cryptography settings in network device models.

questions: what is a yang grouping for keys
how does yang store passwords and keys
subtitle: Reusable YANG building blocks for describing keys, passwords and certificates in device configuration.

tldr.problem: Every YANG model that configures a secure protocol needs to represent keys, passwords and certificates, and without a shared definition each model would invent its own.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9640 defines the YANG 1.1 module ietf-crypto-types, containing identities that name key and value formats, typedefs for DER-encoded structures, and groupings other modules can reuse.
tldr.outcome: Other modules for NETCONF and RESTCONF clients and servers can build on it without redefining crypto data. It only defines groupings, so it has no protocol-accessible nodes of its own.

today: RFC 9640 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2024, and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The related truststore, keystore and client-server modules are RFC 9641 to RFC 9645.

sections.title: Where the Module Fits
sections.content:
RFC 9640 presents a YANG 1.1 module (RFC 7950) with identities, typedefs and groupings useful to cryptographic applications. It is part of a collection of RFCs that together support configuring both clients and servers of the Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF, RFC 6241) and RESTCONF (RFC 8040).

The RFC includes a dependency diagram for that collection. The crypto-types module, which is this one, depends on nothing. The truststore (RFC 9641) and keystore (RFC 9642) modules depend on it, and the TCP, SSH and TLS client-server modules (RFC 9643, RFC 9644, RFC 9645) build further on those.

The document complies with the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA) and defines no protocol-accessible nodes that are config false.
sections.eli5: It is the box of basic Lego bricks for crypto settings. Other, bigger network models are built by snapping these bricks together.

sections.title: Features, Identities and Typedefs
sections.content:
The module uses features so a device can support only the uncommon formats it needs. Examples include cleartext-passwords, encrypted-passwords, hidden-private-keys, p10-csr-format and csr-generation.

There are five abstract base identities. The first three say how key data is encoded (public-key-format, private-key-format, symmetric-key-format), the fourth is encrypted-value-format, and the fifth is csr-format for certificate signing requests. The base identities only define a class of formats. Terminal identities such as subject-public-key-info-format, ssh-public-key-format, rsa-private-key-format and ec-private-key-format name the real formats, and future work MAY define more.

All the typedefs extend the YANG binary type and each encodes an ASN.1 structure using DER. They include x509, csr, crl, ocsp-request, ocsp-response and a family of CMS types such as signed-data-cms and enveloped-data-cms. The trust-anchor-* and end-entity-* typedefs are syntactically identical to their base typedefs and differ only in the expected nature of their content.
sections.eli5: Features are switches for the unusual options. Identities are labels that say what kind of key something is, and typedefs are the shapes the data comes in.

sections.title: Passwords, Keys and Encrypted Values
sections.content:
Several groupings share one pattern: a value can be stored in the clear, encrypted, or, for keys, hidden.

  • encrypted-value-grouping holds encrypted-by, encrypted-value-format and encrypted-value. The encrypted-by container is empty, and a consuming module MUST augment key references into it. A value encrypted by a symmetric key uses the symmetrically-encrypted format, and one encrypted by an asymmetric key uses the asymmetrically-encrypted format.
  • password-grouping chooses between cleartext-password and encrypted-password. It is for credentials used to authenticate to a remote system; the crypt-hash typedef from RFC 7317 should be used for a local account instead.
  • symmetric-key-grouping and private-key-grouping choose between a cleartext key, a hidden key and an encrypted key. A hidden key is of type empty because the real value cannot be shown through the management interface.
  • public-key-grouping has a public-key-format and a public-key. It has no choice for hiding or encrypting, because that is unnecessary for public keys.
  • asymmetric-key-pair-grouping simply combines the public and private key groupings.
sections.eli5: A secret can be written on a note anyone can read, locked in a box, or kept hidden so nobody can read it from the outside. The model lets a device say which one it uses.

sections.title: Certificates, CSRs and Expiry Notices
sections.content:
trust-anchor-cert-grouping carries a cert-data chain of one or more certificates containing at most one self-signed (root) certificate. end-entity-cert-grouping carries a chain containing at most one certificate that is not self-signed and does not have Basic constraint CA true.

Both include certificate-expiration-grouping, which defines a certificate-expiration notification with an expiration-date, so a server can tell clients that a certificate is nearing expiration.

generate-csr-grouping defines a generate-csr action. It takes a csr-format and a csr-info describing what the certificate should contain, and returns the request in the chosen format. Two combined groupings build on these: asymmetric-key-pair-with-cert-grouping for a key with at most one certificate, and asymmetric-key-pair-with-certs-grouping for a key with any number of named certificates.

The module itself has no protocol-accessible nodes, but it must still be implemented, as RFC 7950 describes, so its identities are defined.
sections.eli5: A certificate is like an ID card for a key. This part lets a device ask for a new ID card and warn people when one is about to run out.

sections.title: Example Usage
sections.content:
The RFC builds a non-normative example module that uses the symmetric key, asymmetric key pair with certificates, and password groupings, together with a tree diagram and sample data. Two further NETCONF examples show the generate-csr action and the certificate-expiration notification.

The generate-csr request names the key, selects ct:p10-csr-format and supplies a csr-info value, and the reply returns a p10-csr. The examples use the placeholder BASE64VALUE= for base64 data and the XML encoding, though JSON could be used instead.
sections.eli5: The examples are sample forms filled in, so you can see how to ask a device for a new request or hear that a certificate is expiring.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Several design choices are explained as security points:

  • No CRMF. PKCS #10 (RFC 2986) is used for generate-csr. CRMF was considered, but it was unclear if there was market demand.
  • No key generation. Early drafts had statements to generate keys, removed because there was no consensus on how to identify the key algorithm generically. Protocol-specific modules can offer their own, such as the generate-asymmetric-key-pair RPC in RFC 9644 and RFC 9645.
  • No usage limits. The key groupings do not constrain what a key may be used for. Associated certificates MUST constrain public key usage according to local policy.
  • Cleartext. Storing cleartext passwords and keys is NOT RECOMMENDED. Cleartext key values SHOULD be zeroized when deleted.
  • Encryption. Encrypted values use CMS structures. With a symmetric key, a proper mode such as AEAD or CBC MUST be used so a random IV is part of the input, and Electronic Codebook (ECB) MUST NOT be used.

Access control uses NACM (RFC 8341). The nodes cleartext-password, cleartext-symmetric-key, cleartext-private-key and cert-data carry default-deny-all, all writable nodes carry default-deny-write, and the generate-csr action carries default-deny-all. For that action it is RECOMMENDED to assert channel binding.
sections.eli5: Secrets should be locked up, not left on the table. The model also makes the device refuse to show or change them unless someone is clearly allowed.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-crypto-types in the IETF XML Registry, with the IESG as registrant. It also registered the module in the YANG Module Names registry with the name ietf-crypto-types, the prefix ct and RFC 9640 as the reference.
sections.eli5: The module was given its official name in a public list so nobody else uses the same one.
